_comment: Defaults for `dotnet lambda deploy-function`, so the deploy is one command rather than a line
of flags somebody has to remember correctly.
The runtime is dotnet10, which AWS manages. This file used to say provided.al2023 with
--self-contained, from back when net10.0 had no managed runtime to deploy onto. It does now
(Amazon Linux 2023, deprecation Nov 2028), and carrying our own copy of .NET was costing more
than it bought: the self-contained arm64 bundle zipped to 54MB, and Lambda refuses a direct
upload over 50MB, so every deploy needed an S3 bucket to go through. Framework-dependent it is
The trade is real but small: AWS patches a managed runtime on their schedule rather than ours.
Against that, the bundle is a fifth of the size, cold starts are shorter, and there is one less
piece of deployment plumbing to keep alive.
The handler stays the bare assembly name. The app uses top-level statements with
AddAWSLambdaHosting, which is the executable-assembly model, and that model is supported on the
managed runtimes too - it does not need an Assembly::Type::Method handler or a LambdaEntryPoint
class, and there is no such class here.
ReadyToRun stays. On a framework-dependent build it pre-compiles this app's own assemblies, not
the shared framework, so it costs 6MB and still takes the JIT off the cold path - which is what
the first sign-in of the day feels, PBKDF2 at 600k iterations.
// architecture: Graviton — cheaper per millisecond, and the build container here is arm64 already
// memory: CPU is handed out in proportion to memory, and sign-in runs PBKDF2 600k times. Below 1024 the first sign-in of the day is a visible pause.
// timeout: Catalogue import validates and writes thousands of rows in one request.
// function-url-auth-type: NONE is right: every route except sign-in and health is refused by the app's own session check, exactly as it is locally.
// environment-variables: Set these in the console or with --environment-variables; they are not kept here because the connection string is a credential.
